entities.name: Dafydd ab Owain Gwynedd
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dafydd ab Owain Gwynedd (died 1203) was a pivotal figure in the political landscape of 12th-century Wales, reigning as Prince of Gwynedd, either solely or jointly, from 1170 until his deposition in 1195. As a son of the formidable Owain Gwynedd, who had significantly expanded Gwynedd's influence, Dafydd inherited a complex legacy of Welsh independence challenged by internal dynastic rivalries and constant pressure from the expanding Anglo-Norman power of Henry II and later Richard I of England. His reign represents a critical period of consolidation and conflict within the fragmented Welsh principalities, marked by shifting alliances and intense fraternal strife for control of the most powerful Welsh kingdom.

Following his father's death in 1170, Dafydd engaged in a brutal struggle for power against his numerous half-brothers, including Maelgwn and Rhodri ab Owain Gwynedd, eventually consolidating control over much of Gwynedd. He notably solidified his position through strategic alliances, marrying Emma of Anjou, an illegitimate half-sister of King Henry II of England, in 1174, a union that briefly afforded him significant English recognition. Dafydd successfully repelled several incursions, including a notable victory against the English at the Battle of Aberconwy in 1172, but his rule was often destabilized by the persistent challenges from his siblings and nephews, particularly Llywelyn ab Iorwerth.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Dafydd ab Owain Gwynedd's reign exemplified the challenges of Welsh princely rule in the 12th century, marked by intense dynastic strife and strategic alliances with England. His inability to fully consolidate power ultimately paved the way for the emergence of Llywelyn the Great, who would achieve greater unity for Wales.
